extracted.intended_audience: Businesses, inventors, in-house counsel and patent applicants (and their advisors) seeking to obtain patent protection in the UK, via the EPO, or through the PCT
extracted.subtask_short: UK and European patent filing procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and legal requirements, timelines and post‑grant procedures for filing and prosecuting patent applications in the UK, at the EPO, and via the PCT, including third‑party observations, oppositions, validation and renewal fee rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of patent protection
rubrics_metrics.description: A granted patent (UK or European designating the UK) confers a monopoly right for the term of the patent: 20 years from the date of filing the application, provided the relevant renewal fees are paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 20‑year term is subject to timely payment of renewal fees; failure to pay can result in loss of rights. (Original wording: "Provided the relevant renewal fees are paid, the term of patent protection is 20 years from the date of filing the application.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to apply / ownership issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural or legal person who is the inventor of the invention or subject‑matter is entitled to apply for UK patent protection; joint applications are permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defects in entitlement can create issues before and after grant and in some cases lead to revocation of the granted patent — therefore correct identification of applicants/entitlement is important. (Original wording: "A natural or legal person who is the inventor of the invention or subject‑matter in question is entitled to apply for UK patent protection (Patents Act section 7). Joint applications are permitted. Importantly, defects in entitlement to the invention can create issues both before and after grant, and can in some cases lead to revocation of the granted patent.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum contents and timing of a filed application (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: The filed application must contain a request for the grant of a patent, a written description of the invention including any relevant diagrams (a specification), and either immediately or within 12 months of filing, a list of claims and an abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims and abstract may be filed up to 12 months after initial filing; ensure specification adequately discloses the invention and accompanying diagrams. (Original wording: "The filed application must contain a request for the grant of a patent, a written description of the invention including any relevant diagrams, called a specification, and, either immediately or within 12 months of filing, a list of claims and an abstract.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum contents and timing of a filed application (European/EPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: A European application must contain a request for the grant of a European patent, a written specification, a list of claims, and an abstract; applications may declare a priority date based on an earlier application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications designating the UK should include the UK among designations. Formalities examination, search and publication follow if procedural and substantive requirements are met and fees are paid. (Original wording: "The filed application must contain a request for the grant of a European patent, a written specification, a list of claims, and an abstract. Provided the procedural and substantive requirements are met and the fees paid, the application will proceed to the formalities examination, publication and search phases.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural and substantive compliance for prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Provided procedural and substantive requirements are met and the relevant fees paid, the application proceeds through preliminary/formalities examination and search, publication, substantive examination, grant and final publication of the granted patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must monitor and respond to correspondence promptly and satisfy procedural requirements at each stage to avoid delays or refusal. (Original wording summarised from the guide.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party observations at the UK IPO
rubrics_metrics.description: Following publication of the patent application but prior to grant, third parties can lodge written objections (observations) regarding patentability with the UK IPO’s Comptroller; lodging an observation does not make the observer a party to proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although observations can be made at any stage, the UK IPO advises raising them within three months of publication because in practice a patent can be granted within three months of publication. The IPO provides copies of observations to the applicant and will consider them during examination. (Original wording: "Although observations can be made at any stage, the UK IPO advises that third‑party observations be raised within three months of publication because in practice a patent can be granted within three months of the publication date.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party observations at the EPO
rubrics_metrics.description: After publication of a European application but prior to substantive examination and grant, third parties may lodge written observations (which may be anonymous) regarding patentability; observations may be filed in English, German or French and do not make the observer party to EPO proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EPO provides copies to the applicant (who may comment) and considers observations during proceedings; observations become publicly available if opposition proceedings occur. (Original wording: "Observations may be filed in English, German or French, and do not make the observer party to any EPO proceedings. The EPO will provide copies of third‑party observations to the applicant, who may comment upon them, and will consider observations during any proceeding before it. Observations are also made publicly available in the event that opposition proceedings occur.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition procedure at the EPO (nine‑month period and grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a fee, within nine months of grant third parties may file a written opposition to the grant of a European patent; opposition is centralised and effective for all designated countries. Any opposition must set out specific grounds for objection — patentability, lack of sufficiency and/or added matter (EPC Article 99).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EPO evaluates the opposition; the proprietor has four months to respond (which may include filing amendments). Proceedings can include oral hearings and the EPO may issue interim non‑binding opinions. The final determination affects all designations. (Original wording: "For a fee, within nine months of grant third parties may file written opposition... Any opposition must set out specific grounds for objection - patentability, lack of sufficiency and/or added matter (EPC Article 99). The EPO will consider the opposition and the proprietor will have four months to respond, which may include filing amendments... The EPO may issue interim preliminary and non‑binding opinions... Upon final determination, the outcome will affect all designations for which it was granted.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of EPO decisions on national designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon final determination in opposition or amendment proceedings, the outcome will affect all designations for which the European patent was granted; national designations and procedures will be supplanted by the EPO’s decision if it results in amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any amendments to specific national designations under national law/procedure will be overridden by the EPO decision. (Original wording: "Any amendments to specific national designations under the law and procedure of the relevant country will be supplanted by the EPO’s decision, if it results in amendments.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation requirements for granted European patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Granted European patents must in most cases be validated in each designated country within three months of grant; each country has specific national requirements for validation (e.g., translation requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validation steps and deadlines vary by country; the London Agreement dispenses with some translation requirements for certain countries (including the UK). Failure to validate can prevent national effect. (Original wording: "Granted European patents must in most cases be validated in each designated country of interest within three months of grant, and each country has various specific requirements for validation based on national law, for example the requirement to translate the granted patent. However, the requirement for further validation is dispensed with in certain countries, including the UK by virtue of the London Agreement.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal/maintenance fee rules (UK and EPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: To maintain a UK patent (national or UK designation of a European patent) annual renewal fees are payable to the UK IPO after the end of the fourth year from filing. Annual renewal fees are payable to the EPO in respect of pending applications only (due in respect of the third year from filing and each subsequent year until grant); after grant, renewal fees must be paid to the respective national offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a UK national patent is not granted by the time the first renewal fee becomes due, the renewal fee (and any subsequent renewal fees falling due prior to grant) can be paid after the patent is granted. Applicants must track which office to pay after grant. (Original wording: see relevant paragraphs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and likely professional service needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Official UK IPO fees for processing an application through to grant are approximately £230 to £300, but applicants are likely to incur additional costs for professional services (patent attorney fees, technical expert fees, translations) which vary considerably and may increase if overcoming IPO challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for professional advice and potential additional costs if the application faces substantive or procedural objections. (Original wording: "Official fees charged by the UK IPO for processing an application through to grant are approximately £230 to £300, although an applicant is likely to incur additional costs for various professional services required to support the application... Such fees vary considerably, but will increase if an applicant is required to overcome UK IPO challenges to the application.")

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT (international) application role and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A PCT application provides a streamlined international filing route administered by WIPO allowing a single application to designate many states and preserve a priority date; the international application itself does not become a granted patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over 140 countries are party to the PCT; national or regional applications must be filed in due course for grant/validation in designated states. Use the PCT to delay national filings and preserve options internationally. (Original wording: "This international application system... provides a streamlined service for patent applications made globally... The international application does not itself become a granted patent.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected prosecution timelines and possibilities for acceleration/slowdown
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical timelines: UK national patent about three to five years from filing to grant; European patent about three to eight years. Timeframes may be shortened if certain fees are paid early and correspondence is responded to promptly, or lengthened by EPO resources and events such as third‑party oppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants can use certain provisions to accelerate or slow prosecution; third‑party oppositions are likely to lengthen EPO grant timelines. Prompt responses and fee payments can substantially shorten UK timelines. (Original wording: see timeline paragraph.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Routes to file for European patent protection (designation and filing channels)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a European patent conferring UK protection, a party must file with the EPO an application designating the UK; applications may be filed via the UK IPO or directly with the EPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing filing route (via UK IPO or direct EPO filing) affects procedural steps and where fees/interactions occur. (Original wording: "To obtain a European patent conferring UK protection, a party must file with the EPO an application designating the UK. Applications may be filed via the UK IPO or directly with the EPO.")
